THE CAUSALITY GATE WAS VACUOUS, and my report of it was wrong. I told the owner 'the diagonal sanity arm was a perfect no-op, largest |Sharpe - identity| = 0.0000, as expected because the features are already standardised'. outcome: GERMANY IS NOT A GRID PROBLEM, AND NEITHER IS JAPAN. Holding lambda FIXED and sweeping the whole fitted menu - 48 penalties for Germany and Japan, 29 for the United States - the strategy's turnover, leverage and Sharpe were recorded at every point and the whole curve reported, selecting nothing. The question was whether any single penalty reproduces Shu's published DAX behaviour. It does not. Zero of 48 German penalties are within 15 percent of the published turnover AND leverage AND Sharpe at once, and zero of 48 Japanese ones; one of 29 US penalties is, at lambda 20. The German curve misses in a specific direction: at lambda 4.28 turnover is 1.641 against the published 1.70, but leverage is 0.711 against 0.84, and at lambda 162 leverage is 0.842 while turnover collapses to 0.264, six times too low. So at the penalty where our German model trades as often as theirs it is out of the market 29 percent of the time against their 16 percent: same number of bear calls, each about twice as long. Lambda controls how MANY jumps, not how LONG a state lasts, so no grid can close this. Japan is worse than Germany on the same diagnostic: the penalty matching its published turnover gives a Sharpe of 0.099 against 0.31. SECOND FINDING, from the paper's own Table 3, which prints average shifts per year at six fixed penalties and which no objective function here has used: at equal lambda our US model shifts about half as often as theirs - 6.5 against 9.7 at lambda 0, 1.4 against 2.7 at 5.0, 1.1 against 1.7 at 15.0, 0.4 against 0.8 at 35.0. THE PENALTY-TO-FREQUENCY MAP WAS ALREADY ON DISK, AND READING IT FOUND A FITTING DEFECT. The jump-model objective is a minimum of affine functions of lambda with non-negative slopes, so it is concave, piecewise linear and NON-DECREASING, and its slope is the number of jumps at the optimum. The 29-penalty union refits therefore already contain, for all 256 biannual training windows across three markets and with no new fit, the jump count at every penalty and the penalty at which the fit degenerates to one state, which is where the objective goes flat. Inverting the slope gives the penalty needed for a target in-sample shift frequency from the trailing window alone, so the map is causal. Median over windows, penalty for a given shifts-per-year: at 8 per year, US 0.30, DE 0.55, JP 0.55; at 2 per year, US 4.18, DE 8.60, JP 6.10; at 0.5, US 37.5, DE 75.0, JP 65.0; at 0.25, US 65, DE 185, JP 185. GERMANY NEEDS ABOUT TWICE THE US PENALTY FOR THE SAME BEHAVIOUR at every frequency, ratio 1.83 to 2.85, and Japan between 1.0 and 2.85.
